questions.q: In the worked example, building the re-ranker cost $105,000 over 2 years vs. $131,400 to buy it. What does this specific result demonstrate about build-vs-buy decisions generally?
options: Cost comparisons are irrelevant to build-vs-buy decisions
This result proves vendors always overcharge for AI components
'Buy is always cheaper' is an unreliable default -- the actual cheaper option depends on the specific volume and vendor pricing, and has to be computed, not assumed
Building is always cheaper than buying in every scenario
questions.explain: The lesson's point is specifically that the common assumption (buying a managed service is always cheaper) can be wrong for a given volume and pricing -- you have to run the actual numbers rather than default to an assumption.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say 'speed to market' belongs in the build-vs-buy decision alongside the raw cost numbers?
options: Three months of build time is three months the feature isn't shipped, which has a real cost (delayed value, competitive exposure) that doesn't appear in a simple dollar cost comparison
Build time never has any real business impact
Speed to market is identical to total cost and doesn't need separate consideration
Buying is always slower to deploy than building in-house
questions.explain: The raw cost comparison captures dollars spent, but not the cost of delay -- a factor that has to be reasoned about separately even when the cost numbers favor one option.

questions.q: Why might building the re-ranker be the WRONG decision even though it came out cheaper in the 2-year cost comparison?
options: The cost comparison numbers must have been calculated incorrectly if build is ever the wrong choice

If re-ranking is a commodity capability with no real competitive advantage, or the team lacks the expertise to hit the 3-month build estimate reliably, buying might still be the pragmatic choice despite the higher raw cost
Cheaper is always correct regardless of any other factor
This scenario has no possible reason to choose buy over build
questions.explain: Cost is only one input -- team expertise/risk, vendor dependency risk, speed to market, and whether the capability is a genuine differentiator all belong in the decision alongside the raw numbers.

questions.q: What does the lesson mean by distinguishing a 'differentiator' from a 'commodity capability' in this framework?
options: A differentiator is always more expensive to build than a commodity capability
This distinction has no real bearing on the build-vs-buy decision

A differentiator is a capability that's a genuine competitive advantage worth owning and iterating on in-house; a commodity capability is standard enough that an adequate off-the-shelf option is the pragmatic buy choice
Commodity capabilities should always be built in-house, never bought
questions.explain: Whether a capability actually differentiates the product (worth owning) or is a standard, interchangeable piece (fine to buy) is one of the non-cost factors the framework asks you to name explicitly.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend writing the build-vs-buy decision down as an ADR, referencing Lesson 6?
options: ADRs are optional paperwork with no real connection to this kind of decision
Writing an ADR automatically makes a build-vs-buy decision correct
Because 'we decided to build it' without the reasoning behind which factors actually tipped the decision is exactly the kind of underspecified decision this chapter teaches you to avoid
ADRs are only useful for infrastructure decisions, never for build-vs-buy decisions
questions.explain: This ties directly back to Lesson 6 -- an ADR captures not just WHAT was decided but WHY, including which cost and non-cost factors actually drove the decision, so it can be understood and defended later.
